slides.title: Imperialism, Colonialism and the Globalization of International Law before 1914
slides.text: Lena Foljanty, 19 November 2025.

slides.title: The European century
slides.text: The 19th century as 'the EUROPEAN CENTURY' (Jürgen Osterhammel). It goes along with TWO main forms of domination over non-European countries: COLONIALISM and EXTRATERRITORIALITY — and both spread European law around the globe. Keep the pair in view, because the second is the one students forget: a country need never be colonised to end up with European law.

terms.def: The exemption of Westerners from local jurisdiction, with their cases heard by their own consular courts. The second route by which European law spread — without colonisation.

cards.q: By which two forms of domination did European law spread in the 19th century?
cards.a: Colonialism, and extraterritoriality — the exemption of Westerners from local jurisdiction under consular courts. The second matters because a country need never have been colonised to end up with European law.

slides.title: Early modern colonialism: two different enterprises
slides.text: SPANISH expansion from the 16th century was legitimized by THE MISSION TO SPREAD THE CHRISTIAN FAITH, and what spread with it was CANON LAW, from Europe to America. BRITISH colonialism from the 17th century was driven by SETTLERS in North America and MERCHANTS in India — and the legal answer differed accordingly: ENGLISH LAW IMPLEMENTED FOR SETTLERS, CONSULAR JURISDICTION FOR MERCHANTS. A mission exports a church's law; a trading company exports a court for its own people.

cards.q: Contrast the Spanish and British forms of early modern colonialism and the law each exported.
cards.a: Spanish expansion from the 16th century was legitimized by the mission to spread the Christian faith, and it spread CANON law. British colonialism from the 17th century was driven by settlers (North America) and merchants (India): English law was implemented for the settlers, consular jurisdiction provided for the merchants.

slides.title: British and Dutch colonialism
slides.text: The same slide with the map of British and Dutch expansion.

slides.title: Types of colonial rule
slides.text: The typology to reproduce: TRADING POSTS; SETTLER COLONIES; COLONIES OF DOMINATION; and, as a separate category of European interference short of colonial rule, CONSULAR JURISDICTION AND EXTRATERRITORIALITY. The last is not a kind of colony at all — which is exactly why it belongs on the list.

cards.q: Name the types of colonial rule and of European interference.
cards.a: Trading posts, settler colonies and colonies of domination — plus consular jurisdiction and extraterritoriality, which is interference without colonial rule.

slides.title: The scramble for Africa: two models
slides.text: European interest in Africa increases sharply in the late 19th century, and it proceeds in two ways. The FRENCH model: expansion by FORMAL ARMIES, followed by colonial officials. The ENGLISH AND GERMAN model: acquisition of land by PRIVATE AGENTS under the protection of the metropolitan state, LATER BECOMING FORMAL COLONIES. State first, or company first — and the second route means the empire acquires territory before it admits to having done so.

cards.q: How did the French model of African expansion differ from the English and German?
cards.a: The French expanded by formal armies, followed by colonial officials. The English and Germans had private agents acquire land under the protection of the metropolitan state, which only later became formal colonies.

slides.title: Terra nullius
slides.text: The doctrine, and its two stages. FIRST: the idea of gaining possession by OCCUPATION is transferred FROM PRIVATE LAW to IUS GENTIUM by Francisco de Vitoria (1460–1546) and Alberico Gentili (1552–1608), so that acquiring unoccupied land is legitimated on grounds of NATURAL LAW. SECOND, in the 19TH CENTURY, the idea is MERGED WITH MODERN IDEAS ON SOVEREIGNTY, and 'terra nullius' is NO LONGER JUST UNINHABITED OR UNUSED LAND BUT ALL LAND THAT DOES NOT BELONG TO A STATE. Add the premise that African tribes are NOT RECOGNIZED AS STATES in the European sense, and inhabited land becomes legally empty. The doctrine did not lie about who lived there; it redefined what counts as belonging.

terms.def: Land open to acquisition by occupation. Originally unoccupied land (Vitoria, Gentili, from private law into ius gentium); in the 19th century redefined as all land not belonging to a STATE — and African polities were not recognised as states.

cards.q: How did the meaning of terra nullius change in the 19th century, and what did the change make possible?
cards.a: Originally it meant uninhabited or unused land, with occupation transferred from private law into ius gentium by Vitoria and Gentili and justified by natural law. Merged with modern sovereignty it came to mean ALL LAND THAT DOES NOT BELONG TO A STATE — and since African tribes were not recognised as states, inhabited land became legally empty and open to acquisition.

slides.title: The Berlin Conference (1884–85)
slides.text: A MULTILATERAL conference whose aim was to channel the scramble for Africa BETWEEN THE WESTERN POWERS PEACEFULLY — note who the peace was for. It concerned mainly free trade and free navigation on the Congo and the Niger; rules for the OCCUPATION of territory; and the regulation of the PROTECTION OF THE NATIVE PEOPLES and the suppression of the slave trade.

cards.q: What was the stated aim of the Berlin Conference, and between whom was the peace to be kept?
cards.a: To channel the scramble for Africa peacefully — BETWEEN THE WESTERN POWERS. Its subjects were free trade and navigation on the Congo and Niger, rules for occupying territory, and the protection of native peoples with the suppression of the slave trade.

slides.title: Article 6 of the General Act
slides.text: All the Powers exercising sovereign rights or influence in those territories BIND THEMSELVES to watch over the PRESERVATION OF THE NATIVE TRIBES, to care for the improvement of their MORAL AND MATERIAL WELL-BEING, and to help in SUPPRESSING SLAVERY, and especially the slave trade. They shall, WITHOUT DISTINCTION OF CREED OR NATION, protect and favour all religious, scientific or charitable institutions created for those ends, or aiming at instructing the natives and BRINGING HOME TO THEM THE BLESSINGS OF CIVILIZATION. The last phrase is the one to quote: the civilizing mission written into a treaty as an obligation the powers owe each other.

cards.q: What does Article 6 of the General Act of Berlin oblige the powers to do?
cards.a: To watch over the preservation of the native tribes, care for the improvement of their moral and material well-being, and help suppress slavery and especially the slave trade; and, without distinction of creed or nation, to protect religious, scientific and charitable institutions aiming at instructing the natives and 'bringing home to them the blessings of civilization'.

slides.title: Articles 34 and 35
slides.text: ART. 34: any Power that takes possession of a tract of land on the COASTS of the African continent outside its present possessions, or assumes a PROTECTORATE there, shall accompany the act with a NOTIFICATION to the other signatory powers, to enable them IF NEED BE TO MAKE GOOD ANY CLAIMS OF THEIR OWN. ART. 35: the signatories recognise the obligation to ensure THE ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY in the regions they occupy on the African coasts, SUFFICIENT TO PROTECT EXISTING RIGHTS and, as the case may be, freedom of trade and transit. Read whom the two articles address: the notification is to the other powers so they can lodge claims, and the authority is required so that trade is protected.

cards.q: What do Articles 34 and 35 of the General Act require, and whom do they protect?
cards.a: Art. 34: notification to the other signatory powers when taking possession of coastal land or assuming a protectorate, so that they can make good claims of their own. Art. 35: the establishment of authority in occupied coastal regions sufficient to protect existing rights and freedom of trade and transit. Both address the other European powers, not the inhabitants.

slides.title: What Berlin settled
slides.text: RULES FOR OCCUPATION: EFFECTIVE OCCUPATION, and NOTIFICATION to the other powers. LEGITIMATION: the improvement of the moral and material well-being of the indigenous population; the suppression of slavery and the slave trade; and the CIVILIZING MISSION. A procedure for the powers, and a justification aimed at everyone else.

terms.def: The justification of colonial rule as bringing civilization to the colonised. Written into the General Act of Berlin as a treaty obligation.

cards.q: Summarise the Berlin Conference in two columns: rules and legitimation.
cards.a: Rules for occupying territory: effective occupation, and notification to the other powers. Legitimation: improving the moral and material well-being of the indigenous population, suppressing slavery and the slave trade, and the civilizing mission.

slides.title: Law in the colonies: pluralism by design
slides.text: Colonial law is often based on LEGAL PLURALISM — different and partly overlapping law for different groups and contexts. METROPOLITAN law for colonial officials and settlers. LOCAL CUSTOMARY law for conflicts between the indigenous population, often with local adjudication. And a COLONIAL law DISTINCT FROM METROPOLITAN law for CONTROLLING the indigenous population — with the colonies often serving as LABORATORIES. That last word is the one to remember: measures tried on colonial subjects were not always left there.

cards.q: Which three bodies of law operated side by side in a colony, and for whom?
cards.a: Metropolitan law for colonial officials and settlers; local customary law for disputes among the indigenous population, often locally adjudicated; and a colonial law distinct from metropolitan law for controlling the indigenous population — with the colonies serving as laboratories.

cards.q: Why does the lecture call colonies 'laboratories'?
cards.a: Because the colonial law made for controlling the indigenous population was deliberately distinct from metropolitan law — measures could be tried there that were not, or not yet, applied at home.

slides.title: The universalisation of international law — and its price
slides.text: International law universalises in the 19th century, and the mechanism is precise: EMERGING POSITIVISM makes it possible to overcome the exclusion of NON-CHRISTIAN subjects from international law — a genuine widening. But what follows is EQUALITY as the leading principle for relations BETWEEN EUROPEAN POWERS, and INEQUALITY in relations between European and non-European countries. And the inequality is given a doctrine: a differentiation between THREE TYPES OF PEOPLES — CIVILIZED humanity, BARBAROUS (semi-civilized) humanity, and SAVAGE humanity. International law becomes universal in reach and graded in content.

terms.def: The 19th-century doctrine grading peoples as civilized, barbarous (semi-civilized) and savage, and giving them correspondingly unequal standing in international law.

cards.q: How did international law become universal in the 19th century, and what did it cost?
cards.a: Emerging positivism let it overcome the exclusion of non-Christian subjects — a genuine widening of reach. The cost: equality became the principle for relations between European powers and INEQUALITY the principle towards non-European countries, formalised in a division of peoples into civilized, barbarous (semi-civilized) and savage.

slides.title: Source: Heilborn on who can have a law of nations (1)
slides.text: Heilborn, Das völkerrechtliche Protektorat, 1891: there are groups of peoples which, despite small differences among them, appear to the outside world as A WHOLE BELONGING TO THE SAME GROUP. Within such a group there is always A CERTAIN HARMONY OF CUSTOMS AND HABITS, of religious, moral and legal concepts, and its peoples get along more easily with each other than with those of another group. And the conclusion: ONLY AMONG THE NATIONS LINKED BY INTERCOURSE AND CULTURE WILL A LAW OF NATIONS BE ABLE TO FORM. The argument is not that others are inferior — it is that law between nations presupposes a shared culture, which quietly makes the boundary of culture the boundary of law.

cards.q: What is Heilborn's argument for limiting the law of nations, and why is its form worth noticing?
cards.a: That a law of nations can form only among nations linked by intercourse and culture, since only a group sharing customs, religious, moral and legal concepts gets along easily. Its form matters: it argues not from inferiority but from the need for shared culture — which makes the boundary of culture the boundary of law.

slides.title: Source: Heilborn (2)
slides.text: The conclusion drawn: there is NO GENERAL LAW regulating the intercourse of European states with THE SEMI-CIVILISED PEOPLES AND BRUTE TRIBES of Asia and Africa. And two reasons are given: the differences between the cultures, 'respectively THE LACK OF MORAL VALUES ON ONE SIDE'; and that the intercourse has not yet acquired A SUFFICIENT DEGREE OF REGULARITY despite its new extent. The first reason abandons the cultural argument and asserts inferiority outright; the second is a factual claim about how recent the contact is.

cards.q: On what two grounds does Heilborn deny a general law governing European relations with Asian and African peoples?
cards.a: The differences between the cultures — 'respectively the lack of moral values on one side' — and the fact that intercourse has not yet acquired a sufficient degree of regularity despite its new extent. The first asserts inferiority outright; the second is a claim about the newness of contact.

slides.title: The other side takes it up
slides.text: The part of the story that is usually left out. NON-EUROPEAN COUNTRIES TAKE AN ACTIVE ROLE in the universalisation of international law: the classics of European international law are TRANSLATED into Latin American and Asian languages in the 19th century — the slide shows the translations into Chinese and in Chile — and international law is APPROPRIATED AS A BASIS FOR CLAIMING AN EQUAL POSITION within the community of nations. The doctrine built to keep them out becomes the instrument with which they argue their way in.

cards.q: How did non-European countries use European international law?
cards.a: Actively: they translated its classics into their own languages in the 19th century — China and Chile are the examples — and appropriated the doctrine as the basis for CLAIMING AN EQUAL POSITION in the community of nations. The law built to exclude them became the argument for admission.

slides.title: Beyond international law: codifications as a symbol
slides.text: The context is NATION-BUILDING in the 19th and early 20th centuries — outside Europe either AFTER INDEPENDENCE from colonial masters or UNDER ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL PRESSURE. In it, CODIFICATIONS BECOME SYMBOLS OF LEGAL PROGRESS AND MODERNITY, and European codifications are TRANSLATED, ADAPTED AND 'FURTHER PROCESSED' outside Europe. A code is adopted not only because it works but because having one is what a modern state is seen to do.

cards.q: Why did states outside Europe adopt European codifications?
cards.a: Because in the age of nation-building — after independence or under economic and political pressure — a codification was a SYMBOL of legal progress and modernity. European codes were translated, adapted and further processed abroad.

slides.title: The case of East Asia
slides.text: The lecture's worked example of both mechanisms at once — extraterritoriality, and legal reform undertaken to end it.

slides.title: Unequal treaties and extraterritoriality
slides.text: The OPIUM WAR in China (1839–1840) and the FORCED OPENING OF THE PORTS in Japan (1853) lead to the so-called TREATIES OF AMITY AND COMMERCE with the Western powers — the Treaty of Kanagawa between the US and Japan, 1854, is the slide's example — and to the establishment of CONSULAR COURTS and EXTRATERRITORIALITY. And then the consequence that drives everything after it: RE-GAINING JUDICIAL SOVEREIGNTY BECOMES AN AIM OF LEGAL REFORM. The reforms are not admiration of European law; they are the price demanded for getting jurisdiction back.

terms.def: The 'Treaties of Amity and Commerce' imposed on China and Japan, establishing consular courts and extraterritoriality — Westerners exempt from local jurisdiction.

cards.q: What did the unequal treaties impose on China and Japan, and what did that motivate?
cards.a: Consular courts and extraterritoriality — Westerners withdrawn from local jurisdiction — following the Opium War (1839–1840) and the forced opening of Japan's ports (1853). The motive for the subsequent legal reforms was RE-GAINING JUDICIAL SOVEREIGNTY, not admiration of European law.

slides.title: Translations of Elements of International Law
slides.text: The first students travel to the Netherlands in the 1860s; Wheaton's Elements of International Law appears in Chinese in 1860 and in Japanese in 1864 — under the same title, 万國公法.

slides.title: Japan after the Meiji Restoration (1868)
slides.text: The decision is to BUILD UP A NEW LEGAL ORDER THAT WOULD MEET WESTERN STANDARDS, and the programme is institutional before it is textual: SENDING STUDENTS to Europe; building new LAW SCHOOLS; building a new COURT INFRASTRUCTURE; establishing a new LEGAL TERMINOLOGY; and creating new LAWS. Note the order — people, schools, courts, words, and only then statutes. The Code civil was first translated into Japanese in 1874.

cards.q: What did Japan do after 1868 to build a legal order meeting Western standards?
cards.a: Sent students to Europe, built new law schools, built a new court infrastructure, established a new legal TERMINOLOGY, and created new laws. The institutions and the vocabulary came before the statutes; the Code civil was first translated in 1874.

slides.title: The Japanese civil code in three steps
slides.text: 1870s: the first draft is LARGELY A TRANSLATION of the Code civil. 1880s: a commission chaired by the French legal adviser GUSTAVE ÉMILE BOISSONADE prepares a draft — CRITICISED AS TOO LIBERAL, ESPECIALLY IN FAMILY LAW. 1890s: a PURELY JAPANESE commission is set up, and the Japanese Civil Code comes into force in 1896/98; its 'fathers' are Ume Kenjirô, Tomii Masaakira and Hozumi Nobushige. The arc is the point: translation, then foreign expert, then rejection on the ground of family law, then a code made at home — and the result leans German rather than French.

terms.def: Gustave Émile Boissonade, the French legal adviser who chaired the 1880s draft of the Japanese civil code — rejected as too liberal, especially in family law.

cards.q: Trace the making of the Japanese civil code in three steps.
cards.a: 1870s: a first draft that is largely a translation of the Code civil. 1880s: a draft by a commission under the French adviser Boissonade, criticised as too liberal, especially in family law. 1890s: a purely Japanese commission, and the code enters into force in 1896/98 — its fathers Ume Kenjirô, Tomii Masaakira and Hozumi Nobushige.

cards.q: On what ground was the Boissonade draft rejected, and why is that revealing?
cards.a: As TOO LIBERAL, especially in FAMILY LAW. It is revealing because family law is where an imported code meets the receiving society's own order most directly — the part a reforming state is least willing to take over wholesale.

slides.title: Chinese students in Japan
slides.text: The second relay: after the Chinese translation of Elements of International Law in 1860, Chinese students go to JAPAN — European law reaching China by way of a country that had already adapted it.

slides.title: Summary: a complex universalisation
slides.text: INTERNATIONAL LAW LEGITIMIZES COLONIALISM through the differentiation between 'standards of civilization'. Western law in general becomes the SYMBOL of modernity and civilization — yet in the colonies there are OFTEN DIFFERENT STANDARDS FOR COLONIZERS AND COLONIAL SUBJECTS. Western law was acquired also in countries that were NOT colonized, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; and what was translated was NOT ONLY NORMS AND TEXTS BUT LAW AS A CULTURAL PRACTICE — the writing styles of statutes and judgments, court dress, court architecture. The translation carried OFTEN UNCONSCIOUS OR SUBTLE RE-INTERPRETATIONS, so Western legal knowledge was TRANSFORMED in the process: NO FULL HOMOGENISATION.

cards.q: What besides norms and texts was translated when Western law spread?
cards.a: Law as a CULTURAL PRACTICE — the writing styles of statutory law and of judgments, court dress, court architecture. And the translation carried often unconscious or subtle re-interpretations.

cards.q: Why does the lecture insist there was no full homogenisation of law worldwide?
cards.a: Because Western legal knowledge was TRANSFORMED in the translation processes: what arrived was adapted, re-interpreted — often unconsciously — and applied in colonies under different standards for colonizers and colonial subjects. Spread is not sameness.

slides.title: Reading and outlook
slides.text: Wenzlhuemer, 'Colonial Systems of Law (British Empire)', and Guéraiche, 'Colonial Systems of Law (French Empire)', both in the Encyclopedia of Western Colonialism since 1450 (2007). Next lecture: Chinese legal history to the early 20th century (Li Zheng) — exam topic 14.
